sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Boletus pinophilus Pilát & Dermek, the pine bolete, is a robust bolete. Its cap is often about 8–25 cm wide, dark reddish-brown to mahogany, hemispherical at first and then convex, sometimes flattening. The cuticle is usually smooth; it can be slightly viscid in damp weather and become wrinkled or cracked with age. Young specimens may have a whitish bloom along the margin.

sections.title: Pores, stem and flesh
sections.text: The underside has a layer of tubes ending in small round pores, not gills. Tubes and pores are white to cream in young specimens, then yellow and finally yellow-olive to olive; pressure may cause local rusty-brown marks. The stem is stout, often bulbous or club-shaped, with a cream, pinkish or reddish-brown ground colour and a raised pale reticulum, especially over the upper part (sometimes extending lower). The flesh is firm and white and generally does not change colour when cut.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal species grows mostly with pines and more rarely with spruce, often on poor, acidic, sandy soils. Fruiting is reported from spring or summer into autumn depending on region and conditions, so dates are not a fixed identification character.

sections.title: Taxonomy and caution
sections.text: The accepted name is Boletus pinophilus Pilát & Dermek; Boletus pinicola is an older name used as a synonym in some references. DGfM includes it on its positive edible-mushroom list and marks it RL V (Vorwarnliste, Germany’s Red List watch list); its legend reserves § and §§ for legally protected species. The VAPKO list also includes it under the name Pine Bolete. Brown boletes can be confused: the bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus), for example, develops pink pores and has a dark brown reticulum, but identification must use the full set of characters, not a single image. Do not identify or eat a wild mushroom from a photo alone.

traits: Stout cap, dark reddish-brown to mahogany, smooth to slightly wrinkled; sometimes viscid when damp and whitish-pruinose when young
Small, round pores and tubes, white to cream, then yellow and yellow-olive to olive with age
Stout, often bulbous stem with a raised pale reticulum, especially on the upper part
Firm white flesh, generally unchanged when cut; mild flavour and pleasant odour
Ectomycorrhizal, mostly with Pinus and more rarely Picea; often on acidic sandy soils; fruits from spring/summer to autumn depending on region
safetyNote: DGfM includes it on its positive edible-mushroom list and marks it RL V (Germany’s Red List watch list); this is distinct from the §/§§ protection symbols defined in that list’s legend. VAPKO also lists the species. The bitter bolete Tylopilus felleus can cause confusion: its pores become pink and its reticulum is dark, but these clues do not replace full expert identification. This profile cannot establish that a foraged specimen is edible.
